pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Store separately verified anonymized outputs under data_extra/anonymized/pdf; preserve every original file.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: contrastive distillation of positive and negative rationales, quality-based weighting, and improved student performance and rationales. Greater emphasis on diversity and self-adversarial generation does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning training overhead and dependence on prompt/decoding choices, while distinguishing training cost from deployment storage. It newly explains why teacher-negative rationales may still benefit smaller students and interprets discriminator-score distributions. Section 4.2 also narrows the T5-base comparison from superiority on all datasets to most datasets.

D1.justification: V2 supplies important missing reproduction details: learning rate 1e-5, 10,000 training steps, measured runtimes, task prefixes, discriminator max pooling, masking augmentation, and 500 discriminator-pretraining steps. These are newly documented details, not necessarily newly implemented procedures. The abstract promises future code release but provides no released code.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate SVAMP arithmetic problems, CQA commonsense questions, and ANLI1/e-SNLI natural-language inference. The added analyses use existing datasets and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds the mutual-information method MI (Chen et al., 2024b) to Tables 1–3. It also adds Single-Task to the T5-small comparison in Table 2, where v1 evaluated only Finetuning, DSS, and QCRD. The existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported batch size from 32 to 8 and margin delta from 4 to 3. New diagnostic protocols compare checkpoint lags 3, 5, and 10, fixed and teacher-derived negative sources, and discriminator scores at different temperatures. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct examinations of discriminator behavior (Section 5.5), positive/negative annotation imbalance (Appendix A.1), negative-generator alternatives and checkpoint sensitivity (A.2), and computational cost (A.5). These substantially extend checks of central design choices. Existing ablations and case studies remain; the relocated temperature analysis omits the temperature-1 result.

E5.justification: Section 5.5 and Figure 6 introduce probability-density estimation of sampled rationale-quality scores, absent from v1. This characterizes score distributions rather than uncertainty in benchmark accuracy. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark results.

E6.justification: V2 adds comparator, annotation-distribution, discriminator-score, negative-generator, and timing results. MI exceeds QCRD on T5-base ANLI1, 54.20 versus 54.00. QCRD's e-SNLI result changes from 90.15 to 90.26 in Table 1 and the training-size plot; revised settings prevent treating this as a verified same-setting gain. The temperature-1 result of 67.5 is removed, and the erroneous best-k statement is corrected from 5 to 1.

M1.justification: Section 3.3.2 changes the specified negative-rationale margin loss from max(delta - CE, 0) to min(CE - delta, 0), reversing its contribution under Equation 3. This is a localized objective correction within the retained framework. Renaming self-play as self-adversarial does not establish another method change; implementation changes are not documented.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, related work, methodology, and discussion are rewritten. Section 3.2 is consolidated, terminology shifts toward self-adversarial generation, and discussion/appendix material is reorganized with a new Limitations section. The editorial changes extend well beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn, v1's MinMax illustration is removed, and v2 adds the score-density figure and appendix diagnostic/cost tables. The temperature case study moves into the main text, while the judging prompt and temperature-results table move to the appendix. Benchmark tables gain comparator rows and highlighted winners.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to MAGDI, mutual-information CoT distillation, and SCOTT. Related work more specifically positions prior contrastive approaches as incorporating negative knowledge through model inputs. The overall research positioning and claimed novelty of contrastive rationale distillation remain.

T1.justification: The margin-loss definition in Section 3.3.2 changes mathematically: under Equation 3's negative coefficient, v2 produces a positive hinge penalty instead of v1's negative penalty. This changes optimization direction and is not equivalent notation. The remaining formal framework is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the paper by correcting the loss sign to match intended negative-rationale repulsion, testing generator alternatives and discriminator behavior, and supplying essential reproduction settings. The added MI comparison exposes an exception to superiority, while measured training costs and explicit limitations make practical claims more assessable. These gains outweigh the removed illustration and temperature point, although benchmark uncertainty remains unreported and the broad abstract claim is still insufficiently qualified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QCRD, with the same authors, central framework, and benchmarks. All pages, equations, figures, tables, and appendices were readable and support comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds comparator results, discriminator-score analysis, negative-generator comparisons, and measured training costs.

before.justification: V1 reports original T5-base and T5-small benchmark experiments, component ablations, sampling analyses, and rationale-quality evaluations.

results.title:
QCRD: Quality-guided Contrastive Rationale Distillation for Large
  Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list extend the compatibility claim from PEFT methods to full model finetuning. The conclusion removes v1's explicit claims to be the first such method and first instruction-tuning-specific adaptation. The central claim that bidirectional prompt processing improves decoder-only models remains intact.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds an explanation that retaining causal features helps adaptation relative to naive prefix-LM conversion, while leaving comparisons under training from scratch open. Section 3.3 newly argues that generated reasoning better represents usage and reduces contamination risk, without directly testing contamination. The original training-time and memory limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.9 adds the reasoning-data generation prompts, response tags, teacher identification, and example completions. Appendix A.6 supplies the cleaned Alpaca access link, and Table 9 explicitly lists the default mixing initialization. Most existing implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware information, and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds cleaned Alpaca as an instruction-training corpus. Section 3.3 adds GPT-4.1-generated reasoning data for four existing benchmarks, extending explicit generative reasoning evaluation beyond GSM8K to PIQA, ARC, and CSQA. This substantially broadens training coverage and task requirements; the proposed multi-turn setting is not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds parameter-matched LoRA16 comparisons for every model in downstream-task training; v1 used LoRA16 only in instruction-tuning comparisons. Table 7 adds a standard full-finetuning baseline. These are focused extensions to an otherwise retained comparator set.

E3.justification: New protocols include training on distilled reasoning traces and evaluating generated answers, full-weight optimization, and Codestral-22B evaluation. The timing experiment changes from 50:200 and 200:50 prompt-to-answer lengths on two models to separate prefilling and generation measurements at 2000:2000 tokens on Gemma-2B. Existing main experimental settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a full-finetuning ablation testing whether gains extend beyond PEFT, attention-map case studies for two GSM8K questions in Appendix A.12, and revised inference-cost analysis. The original component, PEFT-method, attention-mask, and mixing-initialization analyses are retained; moving the initialization analysis to Appendix A.5 is not new evidence.

E5.justification: The original three-seed practice, seeds 42–44, and appendix standard deviations are unchanged. However, v1's explicit ten-run averaging for inference timing disappears with the replacement timing experiment. Several added accuracy comparisons also lack the detailed standard deviations supplied for the original experiments. Neither version establishes an increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark and ablation values, including appendix means and standard deviations, are unchanged. New results include chain-of-thought averages of 61.5 versus 59.1 for Gemma-2B and 81.2 versus 79.9 for Llama3-8B (Table 3), and Codestral GSM8K accuracy of 73.6 versus 69.3 (Table 17), comparing Bitune with LoRA. Full-finetuning, Alpaca, LoRA16, and timing results are also added; the old short-sequence timing entries are removed.

M1.justification: The core two-pass feature extraction, learned mixing, training algorithm, and causal decoding remain unchanged. Appendix A.8 adds two proposed multi-turn inference procedures: recomputing the entire history and alternating instruction prefilling with cached causal responses. These are limited procedural extensions without reported multi-turn experiments.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten, affiliations updated, and the discussion reorganized into a conclusion and separate limitations section. Mixing-initialization material moves to the appendix, alongside newly organized experimental sections. Most existing method and experimental prose is retained.

P2.justification: The main text switches from one to two columns, with extensively reformatted tables and pseudocode. Figures 2–3 and the initialization table move to the appendix; the main-text qualitative example disappears while remaining in the appendix. New experimental tables, data-generation displays, and attention heatmaps substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused positioning against prefix-LM conversion and citations for Alpaca, Codestral, and GPT-4.1. It removes the image/video-generation references used in v1's introduction. The broader related-work discussion remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The autoregressive factorization, attention masks, feature definitions, and convex mixing equations are mathematically unchanged. Equation splitting, notation compression, and correction of the answer-length notation do not introduce new mathematical reasoning. Neither version contains new theorems or proofs relative to the other.

improvement.justification: The multi-benchmark generative reasoning evaluation and parameter-matched downstream controls address important gaps in v1's evidence. Full-finetuning, Alpaca, and 22B-model results further strengthen the applicability argument while preserving the original detailed results. These gains outweigh limited reporting weaknesses: several new comparisons lack standard deviations, timing repetition information is lost, and the contamination argument remains untested.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Bitune, with matching core equations, algorithms, and original experiments despite the changed title and formatting. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds chain-of-thought experiments, full finetuning, Alpaca training, Codestral-22B evaluation, and attention visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original instruction-tuning and downstream-task experiments, component ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative outputs, with detailed results in the appendix.

results.title: Bitune: Leveraging Bidirectional Attention to Improve Decoder-Only LLMs

C1.justification: The central contributions remain multi-table database augmentation of query representations and order-invariant hierarchical encoding, with claimed retrieval benefits. The additional datasets and comparisons broaden supporting evidence. Removing the introduction's contribution bullets does not remove their substantive claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for weak LLM expansion results, interpretations of metadata-selection controls, and claims about robustness to noisy metadata and limited retrieval redundancy. Its limitations additionally discuss scarce public enterprise databases, subtle metadata bias, and the relevance-versus-exploration tradeoff. Earlier efficiency and privacy concerns remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-access URL, full database schema diagrams, H&M construction details, an explicit lambda-search range, and identification of DPR for the metadata-category ablation. It removes v1's batch-size-16 disclosure. The optimizer, learning rate, metadata-sampling counts, and A100 hardware information remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds future-purchase retrieval on H&M fashion data using article, customer, and transaction tables. The existing Stack Exchange answer-retrieval and Amazon book-purchase coverage remains, expanding evaluation from six scenarios across two databases to seven scenarios across three databases.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 6 add LLM expansion, LameR, query-table expansion, user-table expansion, and evaluations with BGE-M3. Auxiliary comparisons add reranked controls, special-token expansion, BM25-based LameR, and Contriever-based metadata selection. Naïve Expansion and Expansion with BM25 are retained under the names Expansion with Full and Expansion with Retriever.

E3.justification: New protocols include H&M temporal splits with 24,479 training, 1,133 validation, and 1,124 test queries; H&M-specific retrieval cutoffs; BGE-M3 and reranking evaluations; and within-user retrieval-diversity measurement using overlap and Jaccard similarity. Existing Stack Exchange and Amazon splits are retained. The omitted batch-size statement does not establish a training-setting change.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained pooling, metadata-category, hyperparameter, and efficiency analyses, v2 adds reranking analysis, metadata word-length statistics, a special-token control, alternative retrieval components, within-user diversity analysis, and a noisy-metadata error case. These examine additional explanations, practical constraints, and robustness questions.

E5.justification: Both versions state that results average three runs and report ± values in the main and supplementary result tables. v2 extends this practice to additional results without introducing new seed information, uncertainty definitions, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Matched DPR and Contriever results in the main and additional-metric tables are unchanged after baseline renaming. Extensive new entries cover H&M, BGE-M3, additional baselines, reranking, and supplementary analyses. The new results include exceptions to universal superiority: H&M Contriever Acc@50 is 15.40 for DAQu versus 15.66 for query-table expansion in Table 1.

M1.justification: The core DAQu encoder, hierarchical mean aggregation, query interpolation, training loss, and metadata sampling remain unchanged. Section 5 and Table 2 add an auxiliary DAQu-plus-reranker variant, extending the inference pipeline with post-retrieval reranking.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction's examples and encoding explanation, streamlines the method prose, removes the contribution bullet list, consistently renames expansion baselines, and reorders the analyses. Appendix B is reorganized into a much more extensive subsection structure, alongside expanded limitations.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised, and v1's combined Figure 2 is split into v2 Figures 2 and 3 while retaining its analyses. The main and additional-results tables gain substantial row and column groups. New diagnostic tables, an error-case table, and three database-schema figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references covering BGE-M3, RelBench, LameR, reranking, multi-field retrieval, product retrieval, and heterogeneous-data RAG. These update the surrounding literature and experimental context; the central positioning against textual query expansion and table retrieval remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The retrieval loss, query-interpolation formula, relational-link and attribute-set definitions, and hierarchical mean aggregation are retained. Equation renumbering and rewritten explanations introduce no substantive mathematical revision, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification beyond v1's narrow baseline set through direct comparisons with LLM and single-table expansion, another retrieval backbone, and an additional domain. New controls and diversity/noise analyses make the method's benefits and boundaries easier to assess. Some reporting weaknesses remain: batch size is omitted, new experimental configurations are incompletely specified, and universal-superiority wording overlooks exceptions in Table 1. These shortcomings temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in comparative evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DAQu, Database-Augmented Query Representation for Information Retrieval. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, including v2's image-based database schemas, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds H&M experiments, additional comparison methods and backbones, reranking results, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval experiments on Stack Exchange and Amazon, together with metadata ablations, sensitivity analyses, efficiency measurements, and qualitative cases.

results.title: Database-Augmented Query Representation for Information Retrieval

C1.justification: A central contribution is redefined: v1 emphasizes explicit alignment of vision, language and action, while v2 claims that CDL learns environment dynamics and provides a lightweight alternative to generative dynamics learning. This claim appears throughout the abstract, introduction and conclusion. The trajectory-attention/action-query contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for negative-sample difficulty and CDL's reduced VIMA-Bench L4 performance, while dropping v1's explicit component-synergy interpretation. It replaces the earlier computational and multi-embodiment limitations with discussion of simulation-based evaluation and possible 3D inputs. Appendix A.4 newly explains that direct integration into autoregressive large VLAs requires substantial retraining.

D1.justification: V2 adds a repository link, benchmark-specific encoders, action representations, training budgets and hyperparameters, including the 38M configuration and five ManiSkill training epochs. Conversely, it omits v1's segment/timestep positional-embedding specification, frozen-T5 statement and explicit contrastive warmup schedule. These omissions do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: V2 adds VIMA-Bench, including multimodal instructions and novel meta-tasks, and CALVIN, including generalization to an unseen environment. ManiSkill remains, while Franka Kitchen and Push-T move to Appendix A.10. Thus coverage expands from three environments to five rather than replacing the two relocated benchmarks.

E2.justification: New reported comparisons include DT, Flamingo and object-token Gato on VIMA-Bench, and MCIL, OpenVLA, MDT, RoboFlamingo and GR-1 on CALVIN. Appendix A.9 also reports an unsuccessful π0 evaluation without numerical results. The existing ManiSkill and Franka Kitchen/Push-T comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 introduces substantial new protocols: VIMA-Bench's four generalization levels and 10-epoch training, and CALVIN's ABC-to-D evaluation using the language-annotated 1% subset, five-task sequences and 20-epoch training. It adds a 38M configuration. ManiSkill's reported Gato and VIMA sizes change from 309M/695M to 198M/525M; this does not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 extends component ablations to VIMA-Bench, adds training loss/accuracy curves and with/without-CDL execution examples, but removes the separate vision-, language- and action-negative ablations. The attention heatmaps are retained in Appendix A.3, and the regrasp example remains the same underlying case.

E5.justification: V2 newly specifies 100 evaluation trials per VIMA-Bench task. The existing 50-trial ManiSkill, 50-run Franka Kitchen and 30-trial Push-T counts remain. Neither version specifies independent training-seed replication, confidence intervals or significance tests; the added trial count does not establish increased replication of retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive VIMA-Bench and CALVIN results, including Astra's 97.08% VIMA-Bench L1 success and 3.29 CALVIN average sequence length. Retained benchmark comparison scores largely match v1. However, ManiSkill's 'w/o Both' ablation changes from 83.3/79.4/68.0 to 72.33/76.00/67.00 for easy/medium/hard tasks. Separate negative-type results and several aggregate results are removed.

M1.justification: Trajectory attention and parallel action queries are retained. However, Section 3.3 substantially revises contrastive learning: positives gain image augmentation, the separate prompt/state/action negative families become mixed state/action negatives incorporating augmented samples, and trajectory encoding gains a linear layer after pooling. These are procedural changes beyond renaming the objective CDL.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work and contrastive-learning narrative, renames Actra to Astra, and changes the title and author list. It reorganizes the experimental sections and appendices, moves two benchmarks out of the main text, and adds a notation glossary and several explanatory subsections.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Architecture and contrastive-learning diagrams are redesigned; attention comparisons, training curves and execution panels are added. Attention heatmaps move to the appendix, the generalization bar chart disappears, and the combined Franka Kitchen/Push-T table becomes two appendix tables.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around a distinction between large and generalized VLAs and between generative and contrastive dynamics learning. New discussions include OpenVLA, π0, GR-2 and world-model research such as Dreamer. This goes beyond the change from numbered to author-year citations.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 revises the formal construction of negative trajectories from three modality-specific families to mixed state/action negatives, changing the negative set used in the contrastive objective. The standard InfoNCE form, attention-mask mathematics, connection-count expression and diffusion-loss formulas remain. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1's generalization evidence chiefly concerns held-out object attributes in ManiSkill. V2 directly tests multimodal instructions, novel meta-tasks and transfer to an unseen CALVIN environment, with additional component ablations and stronger comparison sets. This substantially strengthens support for the architecture's applicability and exposes a CDL generalization limitation. Omitted implementation details and unexplained ManiSkill parameter-count revisions weaken reproducibility, but the expanded, targeted validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from Actra to Astra. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions and relocation of material.

after.justification: V2 reports original VIMA-Bench and CALVIN evaluations and retains the ManiSkill, Franka Kitchen and Push-T results, alongside ablations and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original robot-learning evaluations on ManiSkill, Franka Kitchen and Push-T, including quantitative comparisons, component ablations and qualitative execution examples.

results.title: Astra: Efficient Transformer Architecture and Contrastive Dynamics Learning for Embodied Instruction Following

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on learning a conditional confidence gap with an efficient regressor. v2 emphasizes attention and recurrent confidence features, and claims two-stage training is necessary to avoid overfitting. Its abstract and contribution statements extend claimed superiority to supervised competitors, while the conclusion explicitly claims cross-domain generalization.

C2.justification: v1 explains limited short-answer benefits and identifies the strict Markov assumption as a limitation. v2 develops attention-head and recurrent-training explanations, and distinguishes transfer within QA from poor transfer to different task types. Its limitations instead emphasize task-specific training data and distant-domain transfer. These materially revise the mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v1 already contains substantial hyperparameter, dataset-size and compute documentation. v2 adds a repository link, explicit feature-padding and initialization instructions, Algorithm 1 and Captum/LIG implementation details. It newly specifies a 50% PRR rejection cutoff and updates configuration tables and hardware information. The retained LinReg/MLP search grids and reported GPU-hour totals remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage changes from nine to eleven evaluated datasets: PubMedQA disappears, while WMT19 German-to-English translation, MMLU multiple-choice QA and GSM8k mathematical reasoning are added. Eight original datasets remain. v2 also introduces QA-to-summarization/translation transfer scenarios. Table 21 establishes eleven datasets despite inconsistent nine/ten-dataset descriptions elsewhere.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparisons add Factoscope, SAPLMA, MIND, Sheeps, LookBackLens and SATRMD as supervised comparators, alongside CCP, Simple Focus, EigenScore, LUQ and Semantic Density. NumSemSets, MC NSE, MC SE and SentenceSAR disappear from the corresponding comparisons. Transfer and runtime comparator sets also change substantially.

E3.justification: Gemma 7b, Llama-3 8b and StableLM-2 12b are replaced by Llama-3.1 8b, Gemma-2 9b and Qwen-2.5 7b. Sample sizes change, including CNN training examples decreasing from 2,000 to 500. Evaluation drops ROUGE-L outcomes and adds COMET and ROC-AUC with quality-label thresholds. Transfer training becomes QA-only; runtime evaluation changes from 900 instances on A100 to all test instances on H100.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of one-stage versus two-stage training, preceding-token count, token-level versus sequence-level training, LIG attribution features, attention-layer importance and attention patterns in correct versus incorrect answers. It substantially revises transfer experiments. Existing regressor, aggregation and feature ablations are revised; CatBoost and v1's G-versus-direct-confidence comparison are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates for benchmark quality and unexplained plus/minus summaries for runtime (v1 Table 6; v2 Table 4). Neither specifies seed counts, repeated-run estimation or significance testing. Changed runtime values and sample populations do not establish a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Benchmark, transfer and runtime results are extensively replaced under changed methods and settings. New ROC-AUC tables report mean scores of 0.814, 0.806 and 0.807 for Llama, Gemma and Qwen respectively. v2 Table 16 reports mean PRR of 0.238 versus 0.545 for one-stage versus two-stage training. Reported TAD runtime overhead changes from 0.10% for v1 LinReg to 5% in v2, under different hardware and evaluation populations.

M1.justification: v1 learns a conditional-on-error term G and reconstructs confidence using the immediately preceding token. v2 directly trains C on sequence-quality targets, incorporates multiple preceding tokens, and introduces probability-only training followed by training with predicted recurrent features. Direct confidence learning existed as a v1 ablation, but the multi-token, two-stage procedure is a substantive redesign.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, results discussion and limitations. It separates problem background from the method and moves dataset descriptions into Appendix D. The title and contribution bullets are also revised. The changes constitute substantial narrative restructuring beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, removes v1's attention-frequency plot, and adds attention-head case-study and layer-weight heatmaps. The win-rate matrix expands, benchmark tables replace paired metric columns with revised task columns, and several ablation displays move to the appendix. New ROC-AUC tables and an algorithm box further change the presentation substantially.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands coverage of density-based, retrieval-related and supervised UQ research, including CH-Wang et al., Su et al., Factoscope, LookBackLens and SATRMD. v2 more specifically positions TAD around recurrent confidence features and raw attention weights, including an explicit distinction from LookBackLens feature engineering. These exceed bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Both retain the binary-token total-probability argument. v2 removes the explicit solved-G target and reconstruction derivation from v1 Equations 2–3, and revises the confidence and target definitions for direct recurrent prediction. This is a limited formal reformulation; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness of v1 by evaluating its supervised method against six supervised competitors. Targeted training and feature ablations, together with cross-task failure tests, substantially strengthen evidence about the method's advantages and limits. Reporting inconsistencies remain: Section 5.2 says all supervised methods trail MSP on cross-task transfer, whereas Table 10 shows SATRMD ahead. These flaws qualify the claims but do not outweigh the stronger comparative validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TAD for uncertainty quantification of LLM generations. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original PRR and ROC-AUC benchmarks, training and feature ablations, transfer experiments, attention analyses and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original selective-generation benchmarks across nine datasets and three LLMs, together with ablations, generalization experiments and runtime measurements in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: Unconditional Truthfulness: Learning Unconditional Uncertainty of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add an explicit claim of up to 60% lower GPU training time and extend the main performance claim to six policy models. The central DPO-based selective-alignment contribution, 30% token claim, and 16.8× weak-to-strong claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning suffix truncation and amortized oracle costs, diminishing returns from larger oracles, margin sensitivity, and token-selection mechanisms. The shared-vocabulary limitation is replaced by cross-vocabulary support, while manually determined token-selection ratios become an explicit limitation. The earlier math/coding qualification remains in Appendix H.

D1.justification: v2 adds hardware/software, optimizer, epochs, batch sizes, learning rates, and dataset splits in Table 8; baseline hyperparameter ranges in Table 6; the reward-annotation prompt; and truncation details. It also adds a project/code hyperlink. These substantially expand documentation beyond v1 without proving changes to previously unspecified settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use UltraChat-200K, UltraFeedback, HH-RLHF, and QA-Feedback, with Arena-Hard, AlpacaEval 2.0, and MT-Bench evaluations. The QA reward analysis moves to v2 Appendix D/Figure 6. Added model configurations do not introduce different datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds TDPO, SparsePO, and the random-token control SePO-rand to the retained DPO, IPO, RRHF, and SimPO comparisons. Appendix Table 7 also adds TDPO and SePO-rand to the earlier MT-Bench comparison. The HH-RLHF comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds LLaMA3-Base-8B and LLaMA3-Instruct-8B evaluations, cross-tokenizer supervision, and oracle configurations up to 12B rather than v1's 1.4B maximum. It introduces GPU-hour measurements and γ/λ sweep protocols. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a random-selection control testing the value of oracle selection, larger-oracle scaling analysis, γ/λ sensitivity experiments, computational-overhead analysis, and two token-selection case studies. Most original analyses remain, although the TinyLLaMA panel of the token-selection-ratio experiment is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 8 adds error bars and explicitly reports three runs per hyperparameter setting. The earlier three-sampling averages for the data-scale experiment are retained in Figure 4. The new error bars' statistical meaning is unspecified, and no seed values or formal significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial model, comparator, timing, scaling, and sensitivity results. Existing MT-Bench values also change, including LLaMA2-Chat-13B SePO from 6.36 to 6.86; these are revised results rather than established same-procedure gains because the objective changes. TinyLLaMA's comprehensive Arena-Hard/AlpacaEval table entries disappear, while its MT-Bench results remain.

M1.justification: v2 adds a contrastive margin λ to the SePO objective, absent from v1 Equation 26. Appendix B and Algorithm 1 introduce character-based transfer of selected tokens across vocabularies, extending the procedure beyond v1's explicitly shared-tokenizer setting.

P1.justification: Detailed proofs, related work, and weak-to-strong background move into appendices, accompanied by rewritten main-text summaries and proof sketches. The former Discussion becomes separate Conclusion and Limitations sections. Related-work rewriting and the extensive main-text/appendix reorganization substantially change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned into side-by-side model blocks with GPU-hour columns, while expanded MT-Bench category results appear separately in Table 7. The pipeline diagram is redrawn, existing figures are split or relocated, and new scaling/cost tables, hyperparameter plots, an algorithm display, and colored case-study figures are added.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds focused discussion of SparsePO, Inverse-Q*, and T-reg, with explicit comparisons concerning optimization, oracle reuse, and weak-to-strong supervision. LLaMA3 and FlashAttention-2 references are also added. The original three-part research framing and central novelty positioning remain.

T1.justification: Appendix J adds a token-level gradient derivation and the sample-weighting expression in Equations 31–32. The original assumption, two theorems, and their substantive proofs are retained; moving proofs to Appendix C and adding main-text proof sketches do not themselves constitute new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial gaps in v1 through directly relevant token-level baselines, a random-selection control, cross-vocabulary support, and detailed training and computational-cost documentation. These strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. The gains outweigh reporting problems, including conflicting Pythia-2.8B SePO MT-Bench scores in Tables 1 and 7 (3.45 versus 3.65) and a scaling limitation inconsistent with the newly evaluated stronger oracles.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages without uncertainty estimates. v2 Section 4.1 specifies layer-weighted means and standard deviations, and Figure 2 identifies shading as one standard deviation. This adds descriptive variability reporting, without establishing repeated training runs, seed variation, or confidence intervals.

Table 1 reports Pythia-160M cross-entropy increases of 6.01% for AMAD grouping, 7.37% for smaller SAEs, and 5.40% for evenly spaced grouping, documenting an exception to AMAD superiority. M1.justification: Complete-linkage clustering using angular distance is retained, but v2 introduces AMAD-based selection of the smallest group count below a 0.2 distance threshold. These change the procedure beyond its Group-SAE renaming.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, background, and experimental narrative around Group-SAE and three research questions. Separate reconstruction, downstream-task, and human-evaluation sections become a consolidated experimental section. The appendices are reorganized into training, grouping, automated interpretation, feature similarity, and feature distribution, with retained material matched across these moves.

P2.justification: The single-column ICLR presentation becomes a two-column main text, and the method illustration is redrawn. Average bars and causal-task curves are replaced by AMAD/compute tradeoff plots with uncertainty shading, new comparison and cost tables, and automated-interpretability plots. Appendices add feature-distribution heatmaps and redesigned similarity plots; these are substantial display changes.

R1.justification: The new Shared SAEs subsection discusses Yun et al., Lawson et al., and Lindsey et al.'s crosscoders, explicitly positioning Group-SAE against earlier multilayer representation methods through its efficiency-performance tradeoff. v2 also adds mechanistic-interpretability challenges and automated-interpretation literature, while removing much of v1's causal-task evaluation positioning. T1.justification: v2 adds AMAD's mathematical definition and threshold-selection rule, plus elementary FLOP accounting that includes activation caching. v1's indirect-effect and approximation formulations are removed. These change the formal definitions and derivations without introducing theoretical guarantees. v2 also leaves an inconsistency between the squared-error FVU definition in Equation 6 and the unsquared Frobenius-norm ratio in Equation 9.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked a group-count selection rule and evaluated efficiency without compute-matched alternatives. v2 supplies an operational AMAD rule, caching-inclusive cost accounting, and reported matched-cost comparisons across three Pythia sizes, substantially strengthening the central efficiency argument. Expanded implementation details and release information also improve reproducibility. Removing causal-task tests and human judgments weakens direct interpretability validation, and the FVU formula inconsistency limits clarity. Nevertheless, the gains in method selection and controlled efficiency evidence constitute a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same layer-grouped SAE research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and figures, tables, equations, and renamed or relocated material support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on three Pythia sizes, including reconstruction, next-token prediction, automated interpretability, computational comparisons, and feature analyses.

Qwen2.5 configurations replace GPT-J evaluations, and human-evaluation and coherence/diversity protocols are added. improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the benchmark's diagnostic purpose. improvement.justification: v1's broad claims relied on one physical task family without a mean baseline or explicit generalization limits. v3 supplies a more demanding comparative evaluation, forecasting tests, formal statistical analysis, and an informative German-election failure case with substantive limitations.
